questions.topic: Terminating and repeating decimals

questions.stem: A scrap log table lists four measured fractions of a bin: row 1 shows 0.375, row 2 shows 0.333..., row 3 shows 0.4545..., and row 4 shows 0.222.... Which row holds a terminating decimal, and what proves it?

options.text: Row 1, because its digits after the decimal point run out and never repeat
Row 2, because the digit 3 is the only digit that appears in that part of the table
options.misconception: thinks a single repeated digit still counts as terminating

options.text: Row 3, because the repeating block 45 is shorter than the block 22 in row 4
options.misconception: judges termination by the length of the repeating block

options.text: Row 4, because a decimal built only from twos can never be written as a fraction
options.misconception: believes repeated digits block a fraction form

questions.explanation: A terminating decimal has a finite number of digits, and 0.375 stops after three of them, so row 1 is the only terminating entry. The other rows repeat forever, so they need an overbar.
questions.hint: Ask which entry has a final digit that never returns.

questions.stem: A school newspaper table lists two class averages, 0.66... and 0.875. A reporter claims the first average is smaller because the second one has more digits after the decimal point. Explain why that claim fails.

answer.exemplar: The repeating average 0.66... equals 2/3, which is about 0.6667, while 0.875 equals 7/8 and is larger. A decimal that repeats forever has more digits than any terminating decimal, but digit count records how a number is written, not how large it is. Convert both to fractions to compare them.

questions.explanation: Digit count reflects how a number is written, not its size, so a repeating decimal with more digits can still be smaller. Here 0.66... equals 2/3, which is less than 7/8, the value of 0.875.
